extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy, ethics, political theory, and public policy
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of the method and standards by which practical arts (including morality and policy) should be formed and evaluated, emphasizing the relation between scientific theorems and practical rules, definition of ends, and teleological justification. Intended as methodological guidance for legislators, practitioners, and moral philosophers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method for cases governed by pre-established rules (ratiocination)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the first, for example, is the case of a judge, under a definite written code. The judge is not called upon to determine what course would be intrinsically the most advisable in the particular case in hand, but only within what rule of law it falls; what the legislature has ordained to be done in the kind of case, and must therefore be presumed to have intended in the individual case. The method must here be wholly and exclusively one of ratiocination, or syllogism; and the process is obviously ... the interpretation of a formula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a practitioner is constrained by a positively ascertained rule (e.g., a judge applying statute), use deductive reasoning (interpretation of the formula). Do not substitute appeal to underlying reasons when the rule is determinate except to clarify legislative intent where wording is doubtful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislators/practitioners who make rules must consider reasons/grounds
rubrics_metrics.description: The legislator is bound to take into consideration the reasons or grounds of the maxim; the judge has nothing to do with those of the law, except so far as a consideration of them may throw light upon the intention of the law-maker, where his words have left it doubtful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When constructing rules or maxims (as a legislator or policymaker), investigate and weigh the reasons supporting them (theoretical grounds), not merely apply them mechanically. Rule-making requires analyzing ends and justificatory science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground every maxim of policy in theorems of the corresponding science
rubrics_metrics.description: The reasons of a maxim of policy, or of any other rule of art, can be no other than the theorems of the corresponding science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical rules should be justified by relevant scientific/theoretical knowledge about causes and effects; do not assert policy maxims without the scientific theorems that explain why the means produce the intended ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art defines ends; science supplies means (means–end relation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The art proposes to itself an end to be attained, defines the end, and hands it over to the science. The science receives it, considers it as a phenomenon or effect to be studied, and having investigated its causes and conditions, sends it back to art with a theorem of the combination of circumstances by which it could be produced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state the desired end before inquiry; then obtain from scientific investigation the causal combinations that produce the effect. Rule-formation is the conversion of that theorem into a practicable precept when feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not convert incomplete scientific theories into precepts
rubrics_metrics.description: The theorem or speculative truth is not ripe for being turned into a precept, until the whole, and not a part merely, of the operation which belongs to science, has been performed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before issuing a general rule, ensure the scientific investigation has identified not only positive causes but also negative/exceptional conditions that would prevent the effect. Premature rules risk failure when overlooked counteracting causes occur; such cases require returning to further scientific inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize rules are necessarily imperfect and limited to ordinary cases
rubrics_metrics.description: The rules of art do not attempt to comprise more conditions than require to be attended to in ordinary cases; and are therefore always imperfect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For convenience rules are simplified to cover common situations; accept that they will omit rare contingencies. In manual arts this is often safe; in complex social/political affairs it is not, so expect exceptions and the need for judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat rules as provisional; refer to science when circumstances allow
rubrics_metrics.description: By a wise practitioner, therefore, rules of conduct will only be considered as provisional. Being made for the most numerous cases... they point out the manner in which it will be least perilous to act, where time or means do not exist for analyzing the actual circumstances of the case, or where we can not trust our judgment in estimating them. But they do not at all supersede the propriety of going through, when circumstances permit, the scientific process requisite for framing a rule from the data of the particular case before us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use general rules when necessary for speed or when judgment is unreliable, but whenever practicable perform the full scientific/situational analysis to adapt or replace the rule for the particular case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid deriving conduct solely from universal practical maxims
rubrics_metrics.description: The error is therefore apparent of those who would deduce the line of conduct proper to particular cases from supposed universal practical maxims, overlooking the necessity of constantly referring back to the principles of the speculative science, in order to be sure of attaining even the specific end which the rules have in view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not reason down from a single abstract principle to specific applications without checking empirical/theoretical grounds; universal maxims must be tested against scientific knowledge about effects and conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for conflicts between ends; do not apply unbending principles blindly
rubrics_metrics.description: How much greater still, then, must the error be, of setting up such unbending principles, not merely as universal rules for attaining a given end, but as rules of conduct generally, without regard to the possibility... that success itself may conflict with some other end, which may possibly chance to be more desirable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When endorsing a principle as a rule of conduct, examine whether its success might undermine other, potentially more important ends. Policy design must weigh trade-offs and prioritize ends rather than rigidly following a single maxim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present rules together with their speculative justification
rubrics_metrics.description: An art, or a body of art, consists of the rules, together with as much of the speculative propositions as comprises the justification of those rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When publishing or teaching practical rules, include the relevant scientific/theoretical propositions that justify them and specify the conditions under which they hold, so users can assess applicability and exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form intermediate scientific principles relating means to ends
rubrics_metrics.description: There is need of a set of intermediate scientific truths, derived from the higher generalities of science, and destined to serve as the generalia or first principles of the various arts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop and state intermediate-level theories that bridge abstract science and practical rules (survey available resources, enumerate conditions, express relationships between means and ends in broad propositions) to guide practice across varied cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define the end (major premise) explicitly as the province of Art
rubrics_metrics.description: But though the reasonings which connect the end or purpose of every art with its means belong to the domain of Science, the definition of the end itself belongs exclusively to Art, and forms its peculiar province. Every art has one first principle, or general major premise, not borrowed from science; that which enunciates the object aimed at, and affirms it to be a desirable object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before method/design, clearly state the desirable end(s) that practice aims to achieve; this definition is a normative choice and must be explicit rather than assumed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish a single ultimate standard to judge ends and rules
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be some standard by which to determine the goodness or badness, absolute and comparative, of ends, or objects of desire. And whatever that standard is, there can be but one; for if there were several ultimate principles of conduct, the same conduct might be approved by one of those principles and condemned by another...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a coherent ultimate criterion (a single foundational teleological standard) to which all practical rules and judgments are referred, to avoid irresolvable conflicts among competing first principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use promotion of happiness as the teleological test (Mill's claim)
rubrics_metrics.description: I merely declare my conviction, that the general principle to which all rules of practice ought to conform, and the test by which they should be tried, is that of conduciveness to the happiness of mankind, or rather, of all sentient beings; in other words, that the promotion of happiness is the ultimate principle of Teleology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the desirability of ends and the correctness of rules by reference to their expected contribution to the happiness (conduciveness to happiness) of sentient beings, while recognizing that this is intended as a justificatory standard rather than an insistence that happiness be the immediate motive in every action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justify non-happiness-directed ends by reference to overall happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: I do not mean to assert that the promotion of happiness should be itself the end of all actions... It is the justification, and ought to be the controller, of all ends, but it is not itself the sole end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proposing ends that are not immediate happiness (e.g., cultivation of noble character), justify them by showing how they contribute to aggregate or long-term happiness; treat such ends as subordinate or instrumentally connected to the ultimate standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normative claims require teleological doctrine beyond mere scientific theory
rubrics_metrics.description: A scientific observer or reasoner, merely as such, is not an adviser for practice. His part is only to show that certain consequences follow from certain causes... To entitle them to do this, a complete doctrine of Teleology is indispensable. A scientific theory, however perfect, of the subject-matter, considered merely as part of the order of nature, can in no degree serve as a substitute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not let scientific description alone dictate normative policy; supplement empirical/theoretical knowledge with an explicit teleological framework that justifies ends and orders priorities among them before making prescriptive recommendations.
